elements.quote: This is the first edition of a living systematic review of randomized clinical trials comparing the effects of all treatment interventions for participants in all age groups with COVID-19.
elements.reason: States the work is a (living) systematic review of randomized clinical trials.

elements.quote: There is a need for a living systematic review evaluating the beneficial and harmful effects of all possible interventions for treatment of COVID-19.
elements.reason: Provides the review purpose/evaluation focus, but not a clearly labeled explicit main objective or review question.

elements.quote: randomized clinical trials comparing the effects of all treatment interventions for participants in all age groups with COVID-19.
elements.reason: Gives part of the inclusion criteria (randomized clinical trials, treatment interventions, COVID-19), but no explicit main inclusion and exclusion criteria are stated in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Wesearched relevant databases and websites for published and unpublished trials until August 7, 2020.
elements.reason: Reports the last search time but does not explicitly name the information sources (databases/websites) in a structured way for the abstract.

elements.quote: Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool-version 2 (RoB 2) [12,15]. Six authors in pairs (SJ, EEN, JF, FS, CKJ, EB) independently assessed risk of bias.
elements.reason: Identifies a risk-of-bias tool and assessment approach, but the evidence is not clearly tied to the abstract section specifically.

elements.quote: We planned to conduct aggregate data meta-analyses, trial sequential analyses, network meta-analysis, and individual patient data meta-analyses. We performed both fixed-effect and random-effects meta-analyses.
elements.reason: Describes synthesis methods, but does not clearly summarize methods used to present and synthesize results for each outcome in the abstract context.

elements.quote: We included 33 randomized clinical trials enrolling a total of 13,312 participants.
elements.reason: Reports total number of included studies and total participants.

elements.quote: Primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and serious adverse events. Secondary outcomes were admission to intensive care, mechanical ventilation, renal replacement therapy, quality of life, and nonserious adverse events. Wesearched relevant databases and websites for published and unpublished trials until August 7, 2020. ... dexamethasone versus standard care. This trial showed evidence of a beneficial effect of dexamethasone on all-cause mortality (rate ratio 0.83; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.75-0.93; p < 0.001; low certainty) and on mechanical ventilation (risk ratio [RR] 0.77; 95% CI 0.62-0.95; p = 0.021; low certainty).
elements.reason: Provides outcome results and effect estimates (at least for dexamethasone), but does not comprehensively report results for the main outcomes in an abstract-style summary covering all primary outcomes with the number of included studies/participants per outcome.

elements.quote: Meta-analysis showed no evidence of a difference between remdesivir versus placebo on all-cause mortality (RR 0.74; 95% CI 0.40-1.37; p = 0.34, I 2 = 58%; 2 trials; very low certainty) or nonserious adverse events (RR 0.94; 95% CI 0.80-1.11; p = 0.48, I 2 = 29%; 2 trials; low certainty).
elements.reason: When meta-analysis results are presented, the summary estimate and 95% confidence interval are reported.

The retrieved evidence does not clearly provide abstract-style comparisons phrased as 'when groups are compared' with an explicit direction-of-effect statement indicating which group is favored. (While some comparisons and effects are provided, the criterion’s specific 'favored group' wording is not explicitly stated in the abstract evidence provided.)

elements.quote: but the certainty of the evidence was low to very low, so more trials are needed.
elements.reason: Briefly summarizes a limitation/concern about the included evidence certainty (imprecision/low certainty).

elements.quote: Our study showed that dexamethasone and remdesivir might be beneficial for COVID-19 patients, but the certainty of the evidence was low to very low, so more trials are needed.
elements.reason: Provides interpretation (possible benefit) and an implication (need for more trials), but does not clearly articulate broader general interpretation/implications across all findings.

elements.quote: Funding: SJ, JCJ, and CG received a grant from The Grundfos Foundation (Grant number: 2020025, URL: https://www.pdjf.dk/en/). NN received a RESEARCHARTICLE
elements.reason: Identifies at least one primary funding source (The Grundfos Foundation) with grant number.
No register name and registration number are reported in the retrieved evidence specifically in connection with the abstract section.

elements.quote: No evidence-based treatment for COVID-19 currently exist to augment widely used supportive care protocols [7].
elements.reason: The introduction describes the current state of knowledge by stating that there is no evidence-based treatment currently available.

elements.quote: However, a single trial can rarely validly assess the effects of any intervention, and there is an urgent need to continuously surveil and update the aggregated evidence base so that effective interventions, if such exist, are implemented in clinical practice [8].
elements.reason: The introduction explains the importance/need for conducting the review, emphasizing urgency and the rationale for continuously updating evidence to identify effective interventions.

elements.quote: Wehave identified 4 important reviews that are comparable to our present project [77-80].
elements.reason: The discussion identifies comparable prior review projects, but the provided evidence does not clearly and specifically explain the need for the current review in relation to existing similar systematic reviews (e.g., what is updated/replicated and citations with that purpose).
No proposed mechanism of action for any intervention is described in the retrieved evidence.
There is no logic model describing hypothesised relationships between intervention components and outcomes in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: There is a need for a living systematic review evaluating the beneficial and harmful effects of all possible interventions for treatment of COVID-19.
elements.reason: An overall purpose/objective is stated (evaluate beneficial and harmful effects of interventions for COVID-19), but the specific review objective(s)/question(s) are not presented with a clear question-formulation framework.
No planned comparisons are explicitly stated using PICO or an appropriate variant in the provided evidence.

The retrieved evidence does not specify all study characteristics used to determine eligibility (e.g., eligible study designs, settings, follow-up requirements, and how relevant question-framework components were used).

elements.quote: Trials were included irrespective of language, publication status, publication year, and publication type.
elements.reason: The evidence specifies eligibility for report characteristics regarding language, publication status, publication year, and publication type. However, it does not clearly specify the inclusion/exclusion criteria for report characteristics in a fully itemized way beyond that statement (and no additional details such as specific language handling are provided).

elements.quote: One trial was not eligible for meta-analysis, as the results were not reported in a usable way; i.e., the results were reported as per-protocol, and several participants crossed over [43].
elements.reason: The evidence provides an example of exclusion because outcome results were not reported in a usable way. It does not distinguish exclusions due to outcomes not being measured versus exclusions due to outcome results not being reported.

elements.quote: It was possible to perform meta-analysis of 10 comparisons.
elements.reason: The evidence indicates that syntheses were performed across multiple 'comparisons'. However, it does not explicitly specify the groups used in each synthesis or link those groups to the comparisons defined in the review objectives.
The retrieved evidence does not provide rationales for notable restrictions on study eligibility (beyond a brief statement about one trial not being eligible due to unusable reported results).

elements.quote: We searched all databases from their inception and until August 7, 2020.
elements.reason: The review reports the date up to which electronic database searches were conducted (August 7, 2020).

elements.quote: An information specialist searched the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) in The Cochrane Library, Medical Literature Analysis and Retrieval System Online (MEDLINE Ovid), Excerpta Medica database (Embase Ovid), Latin American and Caribbean Health Sciences Literature (LILACS; Bireme), Science Citation Index Expanded (SCI-EXPANDED; Web of Science), Conference Proceedings Citation Index-Science (CPCI-S; Web of Science), BIOSIS (Web of Science), CINAHL (EBSCO host), Chinese Biomedical Literature Database (CBM), China Network Knowledge Information (CNKI), Chinese Science Journal Database (VIP), and Wafang Database to identify relevant trials. We searched all databases from their inception and until August 7, 2020.
elements.reason: All named bibliographic databases (with platforms/interfaces) are listed, and coverage is reported as 'from their inception and until August 7, 2020' for the electronic searches.

elements.quote: To identify unpublished trials, we searched clinical trial registries (e.g., clinicaltrials.gov, clinicaltrialregister.eu, who.int/ictrp, chictr.org.cn) of Europe, USA, and China, and websites of pharmaceutical companies, websites of US Food and Administration (FDA) and European Medicines Agency (EMA).
elements.reason: The names of clinical trial registries are provided, but the evidence does not report any date restrictions/last searched dates specific to these registers.

elements.quote: To identify unpublished trials, we searched clinical trial registries (e.g., clinicaltrials.gov, clinicaltrialregister.eu, who.int/ictrp, chictr.org.cn) of Europe, USA, and China, and websites of pharmaceutical companies, websites of US Food and Administration (FDA) and European Medicines Agency (EMA). We also searched the COVID-19 Study Registry [13] and the real-time dashboard of randomized trials [14].
elements.reason: Online sources (pharmaceutical company websites, FDA, EMA, COVID-19 Study Registry, real-time dashboard) are named, but URLs are not provided for these sources in the retrieved evidence.
No organisations or manufacturers contacted to identify studies are named in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: We contacted all trial authors to obtain individual patient data.
elements.reason: The types of individuals contacted are described as 'trial authors'.

elements.quote: The reference lists of relevant trial publications were checked for any unidentified randomized clinical trials.
elements.reason: The evidence specifies that the reference lists of relevant trial publications were checked.
The retrieved evidence does not describe backward/forward citation searching, including seed reports/citation platforms and search dates.
The retrieved evidence does not report journals or conference proceedings consulted with source names, dates covered, and search methods.

elements.quote: For the detailed search strategies for all electronic searches, see S2 Text.
elements.reason: The manuscript indicates that the full, detailed search strategies are provided in a supplementary file (S2 Text), but the complete search strategies are not fully presented in the retrieved text evidence.

elements.quote: We searched all databases from their inception and until August 7, 2020.
elements.reason: A time-period limit is reported, but the retrieved evidence does not describe all search limits nor justify them by reference to the eligibility criteria.
No citations of published search approaches/filters or descriptions of adaptations are reported in the retrieved evidence.
No natural-language processing or text-analysis tools used to identify/refine search terms are specified in the retrieved evidence.
No tools used to translate search strings between sources are specified in the retrieved evidence.
No description of validation of the search strategy (process or validation studies) is present in the retrieved evidence.
No description of peer review of the search strategy (including process/tool such as PRESS) is present in the retrieved evidence.
The retrieved evidence does not describe any final conceptual search structure or explorations used to develop it (e.g., when not based on PICO).

elements.quote: Two authors (EEN and JF) independently screened relevant trials.
elements.reason: The number of reviewers for screening is reported for at least the screening step (two authors), but the evidence does not report how many reviewers screened records vs full reports at each screening stage.

elements.quote: Two authors (EEN and JF) independently screened relevant trials.
elements.reason: Independence is stated for screening by two authors, but it is not specified for each screening stage (e.g., records and full reports separately).

elements.quote: Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion, or if required, through discussion with a third author (JCJ).
elements.reason: Processes for resolving screening discrepancies are described, including escalation to a third author if needed.

elements.quote: We contacted all trial authors if relevant data were unclear or missing.
elements.reason: The review describes contacting trial authors when relevant data are unclear or missing, but it does not explicitly tie this to obtaining/confirming eligibility information specifically for inclusion decisions.
No methods are reported for translating abstracts or full articles for eligibility assessment.
No information is provided about automation tools integrated into the selection process.
No externally derived classifiers (version/reference), their role, or removal of records before screening in the flow diagram is reported.
No internally derived classifiers (use, training, validation) are described.
No machine-learning prioritisation tools or screening stopping/prioritisation rules are reported.
No crowdsourcing platforms and their integration into study selection are reported.
No information is provided about previously screened datasets used to eliminate records or how they were derived.

elements.quote: Six authors in pairs (SJ, EEN, JF, FS, CKJ, EB) independently extracted data using a standardized data extraction sheet.
elements.reason: Reports the number of authors/collectors extracting data per report (six authors in pairs) and that they used a standardized data extraction sheet.

elements.quote: Two authors (EEN and JF) independently screened relevant trials. Six authors in pairs (SJ, EEN, JF, FS, CKJ, EB) independently extracted data using a standardized data extraction sheet.
elements.reason: Explicitly states that data extraction was done independently (and screening as well).

elements.quote: Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion, or if required, through discussion with a third author (JCJ).
elements.reason: Describes how disagreements/discrepancies between data collectors were resolved.

elements.quote: We contacted all trial authors if relevant data were unclear or missing.
elements.reason: Describes a process for obtaining/confirming data by contacting trial authors when data were unclear or missing.
No evidence is provided describing automation tools used for data collection (including use, training, and validation).
No evidence is provided about methods used to translate articles for data collection.
No evidence is provided specifying software used to extract data from figures.
No evidence is provided describing decision rules for selecting data from multiple reports or resolving inconsistencies beyond resolving discrepancies between collectors via discussion.

elements.quote: Primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and serious adverse events (as defined by the International Conference on Harmonation-Good Clinical Practice [ICH-GCP] guidelines) [9,16]. Secondary outcomes were admission to intensive care (as defined by trialists), receipt of mechanical ventilation (as defined by trialists), receipt of renal replacement therapy (as defined by trialists), quality of life, and nonserious adverse events. We classified nonserious adverse events as any adverse event not assessed as serious according to the ICH-GCP definition.
elements.reason: The manuscript lists the primary and secondary outcome domains and provides definitions for each (including how serious and nonserious adverse events are defined).

elements.quote: For all outcomes, we used the trial results reported at maximum follow-up.
elements.reason: A time frame/measurement decision is specified for outcomes: results are taken at maximum follow-up.

elements.quote: For all outcomes, we used the trial results reported at maximum follow-up.
elements.reason: The methods indicate which results are used (maximum follow-up), but the manuscript does not explicitly state whether all compatible results within each outcome domain were sought.
No explicit description is provided of the process used to select results when not all compatible results were sought.

elements.quote: Wechose to add time to clinical improvement as a post hoc outcome.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports a change to outcome domains/definitions (adding 'time to clinical improvement' as a post hoc outcome).
No explicit reporting is provided about changes to processes for selecting results within eligible outcome domains.
Although primary outcomes are identified, the manuscript does not report which outcomes were considered most important for interpreting conclusions or provide a rationale for their prioritisation.

The retrieved evidence describes data extraction procedures (e.g., who extracted and resolving discrepancies) and predefined outcomes, but it does not list and define the 'other variables for which data were sought' (e.g., participant/intervention characteristics, funding sources) as required by PRISMA 2020 item 10b.

elements.quote: We contacted all trial authors if relevant data were unclear or missing.
elements.reason: The evidence indicates that authors were contacted when data were unclear or missing, but it does not describe any assumptions made about missing or unclear information.
No tool used to determine which data items to collect is mentioned in the retrieved evidence; therefore the conditional requirement cannot be assessed from the provided material.

elements.quote: Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool-version 2 (RoB 2) [12,15].
elements.reason: The specific risk-of-bias tool and version (Cochrane RoB 2) are stated.

elements.quote: Bias was assessed with the following domains: bias arising from the randomization process, bias due to deviations from the intended interventions, bias due to missing outcome data, bias in measurement of outcomes, and bias arising from selective reporting of results [12,15].
elements.reason: The domains assessed by the tool are explicitly listed.

elements.quote: All trials were assessed as at high risk of bias ( S3 Table ).
elements.reason: An overall risk-of-bias judgment ('high risk of bias') is reported, but the rules used to derive this overall judgment are not described.
No adaptations to an existing risk-of-bias tool are described in the retrieved evidence.
No newly developed risk-of-bias tool is described or made publicly accessible in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Six authors in pairs (SJ, EEN, JF, FS, CKJ, EB) independently assessed risk of bias. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion or, if required, through discussion with a third author (JCJ).
elements.reason: The number of reviewers (six authors in pairs), their independence, and a disagreement-resolution procedure (discussion; third author if needed) are reported.

elements.quote: Wecontacted authors of trials with unclear or missing data.
elements.reason: A process to obtain/confirm risk-of-bias information from trial investigators is described (contacting authors for unclear or missing data).
No automation tools for risk-of-bias assessment (including training/performance/validation) are described in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: We used risk ratios (RRs) for dichotomous outcomes. We planned to calculate the mean differences (MDs) and standardized mean difference (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for continuous outcomes.
elements.reason: The effect measures used for dichotomous (RR) and continuous (MD, SMD) outcomes in synthesis/presentation are specified.

elements.quote: We assessed a total of 2 primary outcomes, and we therefore adjusted our thresholds for significance [18] and considered a p -value of 0.033 or less as the threshold for statistical significance [9,18].
elements.reason: A threshold (p-value) for statistical significance and adjustment rationale for primary outcomes are reported, but the evidence does not clearly report thresholds/ranges for interpreting the magnitude of effect sizes themselves (e.g., RR/MD/SMD interpretation ranges).
No method is reported describing how synthesized results were re-expressed using another effect measure.
The evidence states which effect measures were used (RR, MD, SMD) but does not provide a justification for why those effect measures were chosen.

elements.quote: We included trials if approximately 50% or more participants had a confirmed COVID-19 diagnosis.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes an eligibility criterion for including trials (confirmed COVID-19 proportion) but does not clearly describe the processes used to decide which studies were eligible for each synthesis (e.g., systematic tabulation/comparison against planned groups for each synthesis).

elements.quote: We contacted all trial authors if relevant data were unclear or missing.
elements.reason: The review describes handling missing/unclear data by contacting trial authors, but does not provide explicit details on all methods used to prepare collected data for synthesis (e.g., conversions or specific approaches for missing summary statistics).

elements.quote: S4 Table. Summary of findings table of dexamethasone versus standard care. (DOCX) S5 Table. Summary of findings table of remdesivir versus placebo. (DOCX) S6 Table. Summary of findings table of hydroxychloroquine versus standard care. (DOCX) S7 Table. Summary of findings table of lopinavir-ritonavir versus standard care. (DOCX)
elements.reason: The manuscript reports that summary-of-findings tables are provided for specific comparisons, but the evidence does not describe the tabular structures or the specific data included within those tables.

elements.quote: Visual inspection of the forest plot and measures to quantify heterogeneity (I 2 = 58%) indicated heterogeneity. Trial sequential analysis showed that we did not have enough information to confirm or reject that remdesivir versus placebo reduces all-cause mortality with a relative risk reduction of 20% [9] ( Fig 3 ).
elements.reason: The evidence describes graphical synthesis outputs including forest plots and trial sequential analysis, and notes use of visual inspection and heterogeneity measures in relation to the forest plots.
No evidence reports the basis for ordering or grouping studies within tables or graphs.
No evidence reports a rationale for using any non-standard graphs.

elements.quote: Review Manager version 5.4 (The Nordic Cochrane Centre, The Cochrane Collaboration, Copenhagen, Denmark) [19] and Stata 16 (StataCorp LLC, College Station, TX, USA) [20] were used for all statistical analyses.
elements.reason: Software packages used for statistical analyses (RevMan 5.4 and Stata 16) are explicitly reported.
The evidence states that some meta-analyses were not possible, but it does not describe an alternative synthesis/summary method that was used and justified when meta-analysis was not possible.

elements.quote: We conducted both randomeffects (Inverse Variance, DerSimonian-Laird) and fixed-effect (Mantel-Haenszel) meta-analyses for all analyses and chose the most conservative result as our primary result
elements.reason: The meta-analysis model choices (random-effects using Inverse Variance, DerSimonian-Laird; and fixed-effect using Mantel-Haenszel) are described along with the rationale for choosing the most conservative result.

elements.quote: We used risk ratios (RRs) for dichotomous outcomes. We planned to calculate the mean differences (MDs) and standardized mean difference (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for continuous outcomes.
elements.reason: The statistical effect size methods used for dichotomous and continuous outcomes are explicitly reported (RRs; MDs; SMD with 95% CI).

elements.quote: Statistical heterogeneity was quantified by calculating inconsistency (I square) for traditional meta-analyses and diversity (D square) for trial sequential analysis.
elements.reason: Methods to identify/quantify heterogeneity are explicitly stated (I² for traditional meta-analyses and D² for trial sequential analysis).

elements.quote: We conducted both randomeffects (Inverse Variance, DerSimonian-Laird) and fixed-effect (Mantel-Haenszel) meta-analyses for all analyses
elements.reason: For random-effects meta-analysis, the between-study variance estimator/method is reported as DerSimonian-Laird.

While confidence intervals are mentioned (e.g., 95% CI for outcomes), the specific method used to calculate confidence intervals for the random-effects summary effect is not explicitly described in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: Trial sequential analysis estimates the diversity-adjusted required information size (DARIS, which is the number of participants needed in a meta-analysis to detect or reject a certain intervention effect.
elements.reason: Some additional implementation details related to trial sequential analysis are provided (DARIS definition), but other ‘other relevant random-effects implementation details’ beyond the estimator/model are not clearly reported in the provided evidence.
The provided evidence describes fixed-effect and random-effects meta-analyses (and trial sequential analysis) but does not report Bayesian meta-analysis or priors.
No methods are reported for accounting for statistical dependency among multiple estimates from the same study.

elements.quote: Because of the lack of relevant data, it was not possible to perform other meta-analyses, network meta-analysis, or individual patient data meta-analyses.
elements.reason: The evidence identifies planned syntheses that were not possible (other meta-analyses, network meta-analysis, and individual patient data meta-analyses) and provides a reason (lack of relevant data), but it does not explicitly cover all planned syntheses (e.g., the specific alternative handling if synthesis was judged inappropriate/impossible).

No methods are described for exploring possible causes of heterogeneity among study results (e.g., subgroup analysis or meta-regression methods). Although heterogeneity is quantified (I², diversity), the evidence does not report methods used to investigate causes of heterogeneity.
The evidence does not report any subgroup analysis or meta-regression factors/factor levels or expected directions of effect modification.
The evidence does not state whether heterogeneity analyses used study-level variables, within-study contrasts, or both.
No methods for comparing subgroup effects are reported in the retrieved evidence.
The evidence does not describe any informal methods used to explore heterogeneity when meta-analysis was unsuitable.
The evidence does not identify which heterogeneity analyses were or were not pre-specified.

No sensitivity analyses (e.g., robustness checks such as leave-one-out, alternative models, or risk-of-bias/assumption-based sensitivity) are described or reported in the retrieved Methods/Synthesis evidence.

The retrieved evidence mentions that 'time to clinical improvement' was added post hoc and reports protocol vs review differences, but it does not identify any sensitivity analyses that were not pre-specified as such.

elements.quote: Bias was assessed with the following domains: bias arising from the randomization process, bias due to deviations from the intended interventions, bias due to missing outcome data, bias in measurement of outcomes, and bias arising from selective reporting of results [12,15].
